why-types.title: Why variables need a type
body: In the previous chapter, every number in Sigma's telemetry was hardcoded directly into the source file. During an actual flight, altitude, speed, and temperature change every second — you need variables to store and update them in memory.

In Python, the same variable can hold the number `15` on one line and the string `"OK"` on the next. That approach is called dynamic typing: Python carries extra type metadata around at runtime and checks it while the program executes.

Scout Sigma's flight computer has only ~1 MB (1024 KB) of memory (our course teaching assumption). C++ uses static typing: you declare each variable's type up front. The compiler reserves the exact number of bytes needed and catches type mismatches before launch.

declare-variables.title: Creating variables and core types
body: To declare a variable, write its type, name, and initial value: `int sol = 14;`. Here `sol` stores a whole number, while `double battery = 91.5;` stores a floating-point number with a decimal point.
This overview program also shows two more core types that we will examine closely in Chapter 6. The `char` type holds a single character and is always written in single quotes — `'A'`, never `"A"`.
The `bool` type holds a logical truth value: `true` or `false`. Notice one important detail: when printed through `cout`, a `bool` outputs `1` or `0`, not the words `true` or `false`.

When updating a variable later (`sol = 15;`), you do not repeat its type. For floating-point numbers here, we stick to values with just a few digits (like `91.5`) so `cout` prints them exactly as written.

predict-sizeof.title: How many bytes does each type take?
body: C++ provides the built-in `sizeof(...)` operator, which returns how many bytes a type or variable occupies on the current platform. Predict the exact output this program prints to the terminal.
This is a guess, not a graded quiz — you are not expected to know these numbers beforehand. Enter your prediction and compare it with the actual output.
predict-sizeof.explain: On our 32-bit browser platform, `char` takes `1` byte, `int` takes `4` bytes, `double` takes `8` bytes, and `long` takes `4` bytes. On 64-bit Linux and macOS, `sizeof(long)` is `8`, whereas on 64-bit Windows it is also `4`.

memory-map.title: The big picture and typing rules
body: In memory, a variable is a named slot of fixed size. For whole numbers, C++ offers an entire family (`short`, `int`, `long`, `long long` — covered in Chapter 4), with `int` as the everyday default. For fractional numbers, there are `float` and `double` (covered in Chapter 5, with `double` as the default).

Single characters (`'A'`) and boolean flags (`true`/`false`) use `char` and `bool` (1 byte each), while longer text uses `string` — all three arrive in Chapter 6. You can pass either a type name (`sizeof(int)`) or a variable (`sizeof(sol)`) to `sizeof`.

Static typing enforces two strict rules. First, you cannot store an incompatible kind of value inside a variable — such as assigning text `"FAST"` to an `int`. Second, you cannot declare the same variable name with a type twice in the same scope.

Notice how `sizeof(long)` varies across systems: it is `8` bytes on 64-bit Linux and macOS, `4` bytes on 64-bit Windows, and `4` bytes on our 32-bit platform. See the archive entry below for the engineering reason behind this.
memory-map.alt: Diagram: char takes 1 byte, bool takes 1 byte, int takes 4 bytes, and double takes 8 bytes on a 32-bit platform.

more.title: Why type sizes depend on the platform
body: When C (the direct ancestor of C++) was designed in the 1970s, computers varied wildly — from 16-bit PDP-11 minicomputers to mainframes. To let compiled code run fast on any CPU, the standard avoided locking fundamental types to a single universal byte count.

Instead, the C and C++ standards guarantee minimum widths and a size ordering: `1 == sizeof(char) <= sizeof(short) <= sizeof(int) <= sizeof(long) <= sizeof(long long)`. Each operating system and compiler vendor picks a data model that fits its hardware best.

When the industry moved to 64-bit CPUs, platforms split. Linux and macOS adopted the LP64 model, expanding `long` to 8 bytes. Microsoft Windows chose the LLP64 model and kept `long` at 4 bytes to preserve compatibility with millions of lines of 32-bit Windows software. Meanwhile, our browser compiler targets 32-bit WebAssembly (ILP32), where `long` is also 4 bytes.

more.title: What is 1 byte and how much fits in 1 MB?
body: One byte consists of 8 bits — eight tiny cells that each hold `0` or `1`. That gives $2^8 = 256$ distinct bit patterns in a single byte.

In our course, Sigma's flight controller has 1 MB, or 1,048,576 bytes, of RAM. Storing a single `int` (4 bytes) costs almost nothing. Storing one million `int` sensor readings, however, would require 4 MB — four times Sigma's entire memory budget.

first-variables.title: Your first telemetry variables
first-variables.task:
The starter code already declares `altitude` (`int`) and `temp` (`double`). On the next line, update `altitude` to `24` (without writing `int` again) and print both variables in this exact format:
`ALTITUDE: 24 M`
`TEMP: -12.5 C`
first-variables.hint: Write `altitude = 24;` and use two `cout` statements inserting the variable names without quotes.

break-type-safety.title: Break and fix type safety
break-type-safety.task: This program attempts to store the string `"FAST"` inside the `int` variable `speed` — something Python allows. Click «Run» first to inspect the compiler error. Then fix line 6 by assigning the integer `18` so the program outputs `SPEED: 18`.
break-type-safety.hint: The compiler reports an incompatible type error. Replace `"FAST"` on line 6 with the unquoted integer `18`.
break-type-safety.solutionNote: With a compatible integer `18` assigned, the code compiles cleanly and prints the speed.

measure-sizeof.task:
Complete both `cout` statements using the `sizeof(...)` operator so the program measures and prints the byte sizes of `int` and `double` on our platform:
`INT BYTES: 4`
`DOUBLE BYTES: 8`
measure-sizeof.hint: Insert `sizeof(int)` in the first gap before `<< endl` and `sizeof(double)` in the second.

find-type-bug.title: Find the variable declaration error
body: Sigma's fuel monitor fails to compile. Locate and click on the line containing a classic variable mistake.
find-type-bug.explain: Line 7 writes `int fuel = 60;`, attempting to declare a second variable named `fuel`. To update an existing variable's value, write `fuel = 60;` without repeating `int`.

fill-types.title: Restore types and size check
body: Fill in the three missing tokens so the program declares an integer variable and a floating-point variable, updates a value, and prints the byte size of `double`.
fill-types.explain: Whole numbers can use `int` (or `short`, `long`, `long long`), floating-point numbers can use `double` (or `float`), and byte size is queried with `sizeof`.

check-typing.title: What happens when you compile this code?
body: Examine these two lines of C++ and choose how the compiler responds.

options.compile-error: Compilation stops with an error — an `int` variable cannot store text.
options.auto-switch: Like in Python, `altitude` automatically switches its type to text.
options.prints-zero: The program compiles cleanly and `altitude` silently becomes `0`.

check-typing.explain: C++ is statically typed. Once `altitude` is created as an `int`, it cannot hold text — the compiler rejects the mismatch before any executable is built.

drone-memory-audit.title: Sigma memory audit
drone-memory-audit.task:
Write a complete program that declares four variables — an `int` for mission sol (`14`), a `double` for Mars gravity (`3.73`), a `char` for sector code (`'A'`), and a `bool` for active state (`true`) — and prints each value along with its byte size using `sizeof`:
`SOL: 14 (4 B)`
`GRAVITY: 3.73 (8 B)`
`SECTOR: A (1 B)`
`ACTIVE: 1 (1 B)`
drone-memory-audit.hint: Remember that `char` uses single quotes `'A'`, and `bool` prints `true` as `1` through `cout`. Example: `cout << "SOL: " << sol << " (" << sizeof(sol) << " B)" << endl;`.

recap.title: Third mission recap
points: Variables let a program store and update changing flight values. C++ is statically typed: each variable gets a fixed type at declaration.

The big picture: use `int` for integers (plus `short`, `long`, `long long`), `double` for decimals (plus `float`), `char` in single quotes for one character, and `bool` (`1`/`0` when printed) for logic.
You cannot assign an incompatible type to a variable, nor declare the same variable name with a type twice.
The `sizeof(...)` operator reports size in bytes on the target platform (`char` is 1, `int` is 4, `double` is 8, and `long` is 4 on our 32-bit platform and Windows, vs 8 on 64-bit Linux/macOS).
Next, we will find out what happens when a whole number grows too large for its bytes — Sigma's fuel counter suddenly jumps to four billion liters.
